lesson.title: Why Iron Can Be Two Different Ions at Once
lesson.summary: Transition metals frequently form more than one stable cation because their outer s and inner d electrons sit at similar energies, and understanding which electrons are lost first explains why charges like Fe2+ and Fe3+ both exist.
lesson.body:
Main group metals are refreshingly predictable: group 1 metals form 1+ ions, group 2 metals form 2+ ions, and aluminum forms 3+ ions, full stop. Transition metals, the elements occupying the d-block in the middle of the periodic table, break that predictability. Iron forms both Fe2+ and Fe3+, copper forms both Cu+ and Cu2+, and chromium and manganese each form several different stable charges depending on the compound. Understanding cation formation as the loss of electrons explains the mechanism, but transition metals raise a new question: why do so many of them stop at more than one point along the way?

The answer lies in electron configuration and exactly which electrons are easiest to remove. A neutral iron atom has the configuration [Ar] 4s2 3d6, with the 4s and 3d subshells close enough in energy that both are legitimately available for bonding, unlike the clean single-subshell picture that governs sodium or magnesium. When iron ionizes, it always loses its two 4s electrons first, regardless of the order those subshells were filled in in the first place, giving Fe2+ with the configuration [Ar] 3d6. From there, iron can lose one more electron from the 3d subshell to form Fe3+, [Ar] 3d5, and this third ionization is actually more accessible than might be expected, because a half-filled 3d5 subshell, with one electron in each of the five d orbitals, is a particularly stable arrangement. Both Fe2+ and Fe3+ end up being reasonably stable ions found throughout ordinary chemistry, from Fe2+ in hemoglobin to Fe3+ in rust.

Copper tells a related but distinct story. A neutral copper atom is already an exception to the simple filling order, with the configuration [Ar] 4s1 3d10, because a completely filled 3d10 subshell is lower in energy than the more naive [Ar] 4s2 3d9 would be. Losing the single 4s electron gives Cu+, [Ar] 3d10, keeping that favorable filled subshell intact, which is why copper(I) compounds like Cu2O exist. But losing a second electron, from the filled 3d subshell itself, gives Cu2+, [Ar] 3d9, and despite breaking up the filled subshell, Cu2+ is actually the more commonly encountered copper ion in everyday chemistry, including the blue color of copper sulfate solutions, because factors beyond simple electron configuration, particularly how strongly the ion is stabilized by surrounding water molecules and by lattice energy in the solid, tip the balance in its favor.

Not every transition metal is variable. Zinc, positioned at the end of the d-block, loses only its two 4s electrons to form Zn2+, [Ar] 3d10, and stops there, since removing electrons from the completely filled and unusually stable 3d10 shell is energetically much harder, so zinc reliably behaves like a fixed-charge metal despite sitting in the d-block. Silver behaves the same way, forming Ag+ almost exclusively. This is the connection back to periods and groups: unlike main group elements, where the group number reliably predicts ionic charge, a transition metal's position in the periodic table tells you it is likely to form a cation, but not which charge, or how many different charges, that cation might carry. That information has to come from the metal's specific electron configuration instead.
